title: Water wears stone (Avot de-Rabbi Natan 6)
hookLine: Akiva, an unlettered shepherd of forty, sees water carve a hole in rock

cards: A well. A shepherd stops beside it and stares at one stone in its rim. There's a hole worn clean through it, smooth as the inside of a cup.
By the story's telling, the shepherd is forty years old, and he has never learned a single letter. Not one. He's about to ask a simple question about that stone.
And the answer will start him on the road to becoming Rabbi Akiva.

teach.b: The story is in Avot de-Rabbi Natan, an early companion to Pirkei Avot. At the well, Akiva sees the hollowed stone and asks: who carved this? They tell him: the water that falls on it, every day, all the time.
And they quote Job: "The waters wear the stones." Akiva reasons it out.
If something soft like water can carve something hard like stone, then the words of Torah, strong as iron, can surely carve a way into my heart, which is only flesh and blood. So he goes to school.
A grown man, with his little son, sitting with the children's teacher. He takes one end of the writing tablet, his son the other, and they learn the alphabet together.

teach.h: A MAN OF FORTY LEARNS ALEF-BET.
teach.b: Alef, bet. Then Leviticus. Then the rest of the Torah.
In time, the story says, he was teaching crowds.
The water isn't a flood. It's drops. Nothing happens on the first day, or the hundredth.

The stone looks exactly the same for a very long time. Then one day there's a hole. That's the picture Akiva carried: not talent, not a lightning bolt, but a small thing done every day for a long time.
It's also why this path gives you one small lesson a day.

how: Akiva's stone is often retold in Jewish education to encourage adult beginners, and studying a little every day is a common Jewish practice.

games.q: you're forty. you can't read a letter. you've just seen water carve a hole in a stone. what do you do?
o: go sit with the children and learn alef-bet.
hire a tutor to teach you the highlights.
games.why: Akiva went to the children's teacher with his son, and they learned the alphabet together. he became the sage Rabbi Akiva.

practice: Think of one hard habit you'd like to change or build, something that hasn't budged when you tried to move it all at once.

Shrink it to a drop, the smallest version you could do every day: one page, one push-up, one kind text, one minute of quiet. Picture that drop tomorrow, the day after, and a year of days, and let the stone wait.

wordCard.voice: Akiva, who at forty had never learned a letter, saw water carve a stone and reasoned: if water can do that, words of Torah can carve my heart.

orig.note: Hebrew, Job 14:19: the waters wear the stones.
